rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣirāṭ means a path and derives from swallowing; its root evokes the path consuming its traveler or the traveler consuming it.
rows.anchor: والصراط ( الطريق وأصله بالسين من السرط وهو اللقم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir and Yaʿqub transmit the original sīn; most readers use the Qurayshi ṣād, Hamza colors ṣād toward zāy, and pure zāy is attributed to ʿUdhr and Kalb; Alusi judges ṣād most eloquent.
rows.anchor: وبالسين على الأصل قرأ إبن كثير برواية قنبل ورويس اللؤلؤي عن يعقوب وقرأ الجمهور بالصاد وهي لغة قريش وقرأ حمزة بإشمام الصاد زايا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hijaz speakers treat ṣirāṭ as feminine, Tamim speakers as masculine; masculine use is more common, with plural patterns depending on gender.
rows.anchor: وأهل الحجاز يؤنثون الصراط كالطريق والسبيل والزقاق والسوق وبنو تميم يذكرون هذا كله وتذكيره هو الأكثر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-mustaqīm is level and without crookedness.
rows.anchor: و ( المستقيم ( المستوي الذي لا إعوجاج فيه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One reported interpretation identifies the straight path as the true path.
rows.anchor: وأختلف في المراد منه فقيل الطريق الحق وقيل ملة الإسلام

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other reported interpretations identify it with Islam or the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: وقيل ملة الإسلام وقيل القرآن

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi rejects the Islam and Qur'an readings because the people blessed in 1:7 include earlier nations who had neither; Alusi objects that al-Razi elsewhere defines the path by universal moral moderation.
rows.anchor: ردهما الرازي قدس سره بأن قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reported view makes the path knowledge of how each thing points to the divine essence and attributes.
rows.anchor: وقيل المراد به معرفة ما في كل شيء من كيفية دلالته على الذات والصفات

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view makes it the early peoples’ path of enduring great hardships for God's pleasure.
rows.anchor: وقيل المراد منه صراط الأولين في تحمل المشاق العظيمة لأجل مرضاة الله تعالى

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further view identifies the path with worship, citing God's command to worship Him; Alusi says Qur'anic passages interpret one another but finds this argument questionable.
rows.anchor: وقيل العبادة لقوله تعالى ( وأن أعبدوني هذا صراط مستقيم )

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another reported interpretation is turning away from everything besides God and devoting oneself wholly to Him.
rows.anchor: وقيل هو الإعراض عن السوي والإقبال بالكلية على المولى

rows.speaker: الشيخ الأكبر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿArabi defines the straight path as the establishment of tawhid in both union and distinction.
rows.anchor: وقال الشيخ الأكبر قدس سره وهو ثبوت التوحيد في الجمع والتفرقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi distinguishes a general path for everyone from a special path for spiritual elect; both belong to the paths of those blessed according to their ranks.
rows.anchor: فالأول جسر بين العبد وبين الله سبحانه ممدود على متن جهنم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The general path is the revealed law in knowledge, action, character, and spiritual state, imaged as a bridge over the hell of disbelief, sin, ignorance, innovation, and desire; its afterlife form reflects one's present state.
rows.anchor: وهو الإستقامة على ما ورد به الشرع الشريف القويم علما وعملا وخلقا وحالا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The special path is arrival at God: seeing creatures as without independent action, then life, then as sheer nonbeing; further travel in God is endless because divine beauty and majesty are inexhaustible.
rows.anchor: ومن شهد الخلق لا فعل لهم فقد فاز ومن شهدهم لا حياة لهم فقد جاز ومن شهدهم عين العدم فقد وصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Prophetic report says a veil or cloud comes over his heart and that he seeks God's forgiveness seventy times daily; Alusi uses it to illustrate ongoing spiritual ascent.
rows.anchor: إنه ليغان على قلبي فأستغفر الله في اليوم والليلة سبعين مرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For ordinary believers the prayer asks guidance to obey commands and avoid prohibitions; for spiritual elect it asks steadfastness in gifts already received, a reading attributed to ʿAli and Ubayy.
rows.anchor: متى قال العامي أهدنا الصراط المستقيم أراد أرشدنا إلى الإستقامة على إمتثال أوامرك

rows.speaker: يعسوب المؤمنين وأبي
rows.claim: The special interpretation—asking to be kept firm in what one has been granted—is transmitted from ʿAli and Ubayy.
rows.anchor: وهو المروي عن يعسوب المؤمنين كرم الله تعالى وجهه وأبي رضي الله تعالى عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A seeker must perfect and become firmly established in each station before moving to the next, so asking for continued firmness advances spiritual progress.
rows.anchor: ولا ينتقل إلى مقام أو حال إلا بعد الرسوخ فيما تحته والثبات عليه

rows.speaker: المحققين
rows.claim: One answer to why the already guided ask for guidance is that they seek protection from doubts and deviation, as in the prayer of 3:8 and the hadith asking the Turner of hearts for firmness.
rows.anchor: أحدها أن معناه ثبتنا على الدين كيلا تزلزلنا الشبه

rows.speaker: المحققين
rows.claim: A second answer is that believers seek an increase in guidance, as promised in 47:17.
rows.anchor: وثانيها أعطنا زيادة الهدى كما قال تعالى : ( والذين أهتدوا زادهم هدى )

rows.speaker: المحققين
rows.claim: A third answer interprets guidance as reward: believers ask to be led to Paradise, supported by 10:9 and 7:43.
rows.anchor: وثالثها أن الهداية الثواب كقوله تعالى ( يهديهم ربهم بإيمانهم )

rows.speaker: المحققين
rows.claim: A fourth answer asks God to keep guiding believers to truth in the future as He guided them in the past.
rows.anchor: ورابعها أن المراد دلنا على الحق في مستقبل عمرنا كما دللتنا عليه في ماضيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi relates the request for guidance to the preceding request for aid through four combinations of broad or specific aid and broad or specific meanings of the path; in one combination guidance singles out the greatest aim from all needs.
rows.anchor: بقى الكلام في ربط هذه الجملة بما قبلها وقد قيل أن عندنا إحتمالات أربعة

rows.speaker: الحسن والضحاك وزيد بن علي
rows.claim: Al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, and Zayd ibn ʿAli read ṣirāṭan mustaqīman without the definite article; Jaʿfar al-Sadiq reads ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm in an annexation, while the canonical reading is the wording given.
rows.anchor: وقد قرأ الحسن والضحاك وزيد بن علي صراطا مستقيما دون تعريف وقرأ جعفر الصادق صراط المستقيم بالإضافة والمتواتر ما تلوناه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second ṣirāṭ is a complete appositive for the first; apposition reinforces the relation and explains the straight path as the path of Muslims, powerfully affirming its soundness.
rows.anchor: بدل من الصراط الأول بدل الكل من الكل وهو الذي يسميه إبن مالك

rows.speaker: إبن مالك
rows.claim: Ibn Malik calls this a matching apposition to avoid calling God part of a whole in phrases such as the path of God.
rows.anchor: وهو الذي يسميه إبن مالك البدل الموافق أو المطابق تحاشيا من إطلاق الكل على الله تعالى

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some take the second path as an adjective; an unusual report treats it as distinct from the first and offers several interpretations.
rows.anchor: وقيل صفة له ومن غريب المنقول أن الصراط الثاني غير الأول

rows.speaker: جعفر بن محمد
rows.claim: Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad interprets the second path as knowledge of God and understanding from Him.
rows.anchor: فمن جعفر بن محمد هو العلم بالله والفهم عنه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other reported interpretations make it inward agreement with outward gratitude, or observance of religious duties and sunnas; Alusi dismisses the latter as a departure from the straight path.
rows.anchor: وقيل موافقة الباطن للظاهر في إسباغ النعمة وقيل إلتزام الفرائض والسنن ولايخفى أن هذا القول خروج عن الصراط المستقيم

rows.speaker: إبن مسعود وزيد بن علي
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿud and Zayd ibn ʿAli read “the path of those whom You favored” as “the path of whom You favored”; the reading is also transmitted from ʿUmar and the Prophet's Household.
rows.anchor: وقرأ إبن مسعود وزيد بن علي صراط من أنعمت عليهم وهو المروي عن عمر وأهل البيت

rows.speaker: الشهاب
rows.claim: Al-Shihab infers that the variant allows ambiguous names such as “who” to be applied to God; Alusi says the inference is mistaken because the annexed pronoun is the object, not agent, of the favor.
rows.anchor: قال الشهاب : وفيه دليل على جواز إطلاق الأسماء المبهمة ( كمن ) على الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Divine favor is conveying benefit to rational beings; hence one does not say that God favored a horse, and the blessing is defined as an unmotivated benefit to a human.
rows.anchor: والأنعام إيصال الإحسان إلى الغير من العقلاء كما قاله الراغب فلا يقال أنعم على فرسه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Reported identifications of the favored include believers generally, prophets, the followers of Moses and Jesus before textual alteration and abrogation, Muhammad's Companions, or Muhammad with Abu Bakr and ʿUmar.
rows.anchor: وأختلف في هؤلاء المنعم عليهم فقيل المؤمنون مطلقا وقيل الأنبياء وقيل أصحاب موسى وعيسى

rows.speaker: إبن عباس
rows.claim: Alusi prefers Ibn ʿAbbas's broad interpretation: prophets, angels, martyrs, the truthful, and everyone who obeys and worships God, as in 4:69; the unqualified blessing embraces God's innumerable favors.
rows.anchor: عن إبن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما أن المراد بالذين أنعمت عليهم الأنبياء والملائكة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other explanations say God favored them by creating them for felicity, saving them from destruction, or guiding them.
rows.anchor: وقيل أنعم عليهم بخلقهم للسعادة وقيل بأن نجاهم من الهلكة وقيل بالهداية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first-person past tense “You favored” appeals tenderly to God's prior favor and asks Him to complete it by answering the prayer for guidance.
rows.anchor: وفي بناء أنعمت للفاعل إستعطاف فكأن الداعي يقول أطلب منك الهداية إذ سبق إنعامك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source lists ten transmitted pronunciations of عليهم, including variants in vowel on the hāʾ and mīm, whether mīm is still or followed by a vowel or glide.
rows.anchor: وحكى اللغويون في ( عليهم ) عشر لغات ضم الهاء وإسكان الميم وهي قراءة حمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The remaining transmitted forms of عليهم vary the hāʾ and mīm vowels and whether a following wāw or yāʾ is pronounced; named transmitters include al-Aʿraj, Muslim ibn Jundub, Ibn Hurmuz, and others.
rows.anchor: وهي قراءة الأعرج ومسلم بن جندب وجماعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The set of ten forms comprises combinations of still, lengthened, or unlengthened mīm and differing hāʾ/mīm vowels; their arguments are treated in grammar books.
rows.anchor: وحاصلها ضم الهاء مع سكون الميم أو ضمها بإشباع أو دونه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Other than those who incurred anger” is a complete appositive for “those whom You favored”; taking it as an appositive for their pronoun is semantically awkward, though the relative clause remains grammatically attached.
rows.anchor: ( غير المغضوب عليهم ولا الضالين ( بدل من الذين بدل كل من كل

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh treats ghayr as an explanatory or restrictive adjective of “those”; Alusi argues the partly specified group can function like an indefinite despite the relative phrase's definiteness.
rows.anchor: وعن سيبويه أنها صفة الذين مبينة أو مقيدة

rows.speaker: العلامة الساليكوتي
rows.claim: Al-Salikuti and others offer an analysis of ghayr's definiteness through the partly specified group; Alusi says their explanation has a difficulty.
rows.anchor: قاله العلامة الساليكوتي وغيره ولايخلو عن دغدغة

rows.speaker: المحققين من علماء العربية
rows.claim: Alusi adopts the view that ghayr can become definite by annexation when it lies between two definite opposites, such as motion and stillness; another rule permits definiteness when the annexed term has one opposite.
rows.anchor: أن ( غير ) هنا معرفة لأن المحققين من علماء العربية قالوا إنها قد تتعرف بالإضافة

rows.speaker: عمر إبن الخطاب
rows.claim: ʿUmar read ghayra in the accusative; it is also transmitted irregularly from Ibn Kathir, most plausibly as a circumstantial accusative referring to the pronoun in “upon them.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ عمر إبن الخطاب رضي الله تعالى عنه ( غير ) بالنصب وروى ذلك شاذا عن إبن كثير

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash allows the accusative as a connected or disconnected exception if “favor” is broad; al-Farraʾ forbids joining negative lā to an exceptive phrase meaning “other than.”
rows.anchor: الأخفش أن يكون النصب على الإستثنأء المنقطع أو المتصل إن فسر الأنعام بما يعم

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil's analysis, which Alusi endorses, supplies an omitted verb meaning “I mean”; Alusi rejects the circumstantial analysis because it requires indefiniteness or a strained sense of ghayr.
rows.anchor: وعند الخليل النصب بفعل محذوف أعني أعني وبه أقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative analysis supplies “path” before “those who incurred anger,” but Alusi prefers avoiding ellipsis; the supplied phrase could then be adjective, apposition, or circumstantial.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم في الآية حذف والتقدير غير صراط المغضوب عليهم وهو ممكن على هذه القراءة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source gives several technical definitions of anger: a movement arising from desire for vengeance, the will to exact vengeance, or an inward condition producing outward movement; a report likens anger to a glowing ember in the heart.
rows.anchor: وفسر تارة بحركة للنفس مبدؤها إرادة الإنتقام كما في شرح المفتاح للسعد

rows.speaker: الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari explains God's anger as His will to exact vengeance and punish sinners, acting as an angry ruler acts toward a subordinate.
rows.anchor: وفي الكشاف معنى غضب الله تعالى إرادة الإنتقام من العصاة وإنزال العقوبة بهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi follows the early community: anger is a divine attribute befitting God, whose reality and manner are unknown, like mercy; “My mercy precedes My anger” concerns the greater or earlier manifestation of mercy.
rows.anchor: قال سلف الأمة هو صفة لله تعالى لائقة بجلال ذاته لا أعلم حقيقتها ولا كيف هي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍalāl originally means destruction, as in 32:10, and in religion means departure from truth; the text also cites a usage where God “destroys” deeds.
rows.anchor: وأصل الضلال الهلاك ومنه قوله تعالى : ( أئذا ضللنا في الأرض ) أي هلكنا

rows.speaker: أبو أيوب السختياني
rows.claim: Abu Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani read the alif of wa-lā al-ḍāllīn as hamza to avoid adjacent quiescent letters, although that meeting is allowed; comparable dialect forms and a line of poetry are cited.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو أيوب السختياني ( ولا الضالين ) بإبدال الألف همزة

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب وعبدالله بن الزبير
rows.claim: A reading attributed to ʿUmar and ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr adds ghayr before “those astray”; the canonical reading is otherwise, and al-Kufis treat ghayr as negation reinforcing the phrase.
rows.anchor: وروى عن عمر بن الخطاب رضي الله تعالى عنه وعبدالله بن الزبير أنهما كانا يقرآن وغير الضالين والمتواتر لا

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: The Prophet identifies those under anger as Jews and those astray as Christians; Ahmad transmits it and Ibn Hibban grades it sound, and Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Masʿud also transmit the interpretation.
rows.anchor: وقد روى ذلك أحمد في مسنده وحسنه إبن حبان في صحيحه مرفوعا إلى رسول الله

rows.speaker: إبن أبي حاتم
rows.claim: Ibn Abi Hatim says he knows no disagreement among exegetes that the angry are Jews and the astray are Christians; Alusi rejects replacing this with generic categories of sinners and doctrinally mistaken people.
rows.anchor: وقال إبن أبي حاتم : لا أعلم فيه خلافا للمفسرين

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi proposes that the angry are unbelievers and the astray are hypocrites, paralleling the opening of al-Baqara; Alusi rejects the analogy against the Prophet's explicit report.
rows.anchor: أنه زاد في الشطرنج بغلا فقال ويحتمل أن يقال المغضوب عليهم هم الكفار والضالون هم المنافقون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur'anic citations can support the Jewish and Christian identifications, but anger and straying also describe unbelievers generally; Alusi says the hadith is the better proof.
rows.anchor: والأولى الإستدلال بالحديث لأن الغضب والضلال وردا جميعا في القرآن لجميع الكفار على العموم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angry are named before those astray because Jews preceded Christians historically; alternatively, favor contrasts semantically with retribution, or Jews are more hostile and corrupt.
rows.anchor: وإنما قدم سبحانه المغضوب عليهم على الضالين مع أن الضلال في باديء النظر سبب للغضب

rows.speaker: السلفي والديلمي وإبن عدي
rows.claim: A report says whoever lacks charity should curse the Jews; Alusi cites it in support of judging Jewish hostility more severe than that of Christians.
rows.anchor: وورد في الحديث من لم يكن عنده صدقة فليلعن اليهود رواه السلفي والديلمي وإبن عدي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi argues Jews rejected both Jesus and Muhammad, whereas Christians rejected Muhammad; he also rejects the claim that Christian trinitarianism is worse than Jewish claims that God is poor, constrained, or has a son.
rows.anchor: مما يدل على أن اليهود أسوأ حالا من النصارى أنهم كفروا بنبيين محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم وعيسى عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi says the claim that Christians are worse, based on “Dalāʾil al-asrār,” mistakes signs' inner meanings and cannot be settled by blind imitation because this is not a subsidiary legal question.
rows.anchor: وقول النصارى بالتثليث ليس أفظع من قول اليهود إن الله فقير ونحن أغنياء

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some say “those astray” comes last to match the verse endings; Alusi allows this as one factor but rejects it as a sufficient explanation by itself.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم : تأخير الضالين لموافقة رؤوس الآي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is directly credited with favor to draw near in prayer, but anger is phrased impersonally as a matter of decorum; the supplicant seeks a path whose blessing is already established.
rows.anchor: وإنما أسند النعمة إليه تعالى تقربا والمقصود طلب الهداية إلى صراط من ثبت إنعام الله تعالى عليه

rows.speaker: إبن كثير والتنوخي
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir and al-Tanukhi classify passive wording after direct address as an unusual kind of rhetorical turn; Alusi says this fits older “variegation” usage, or can be called a turn under al-Sakkaki's broader definition.
rows.anchor: وقد عد إبن كثير في كنز البلاغة والتنوخي في الأقصى للقريب بناء الفعل للمفعول بعد خطاب فاعله

rows.speaker: أبو ميسرة
rows.claim: Abu Maysara reports that Gabriel taught the Prophet to say amin after al-Fatiha; the Prophet then said it.
rows.anchor: فقد روى إبن أبي شيبة في مصنفه والبيهقي في الدلائل عن أبي ميسرة أن جبريل أقرأ النبي

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: The Prophet instructed congregants to say amin after the imam recites the ending of al-Fatiha, saying God will love them; Hanafis say it quietly, while Shafiʿis say it aloud.
rows.anchor: إذا قرأ يعني الإمام غير المغضوب عليهم ولا الضالين فقولوا آمين يحبكم الله

rows.speaker: علي وعبدالله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Quiet amin is attributed to ʿAli and Ibn Masʿud and is the Hanafi position; Shafiʿis vocalize it, Hasan says the imam should omit it, and one uncommon report from Abu Hanifa also favors concealment.
rows.anchor: وإخفاؤها مذهب ساداتنا الحنفية وهو مذهب أمير المؤمنين علي كرم الله تعالى وجهه وعبدالله بن مسعود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Amin is not part of the Qur'an by consensus, so a brief pause separates it from the next sura; the view attributed to Mujahid that it belongs to al-Fatiha is false.
rows.anchor: وليست من القرآن إجماعا ولذا سن الفصل بينها وبين السورة بسكتة لطيفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Amin is an Arabic indeclinable imperative-noun meaning “respond”; other views call it broader in meaning, foreign, a divine name, or a form with a doubled mīm, which the source discusses and disputes.
rows.anchor: والصحيح أنها كلمة عربية ومعناها أستجيب وقيل موضوعة لما هو أعم منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A sound report from Abu Hurayra says the Prophet taught Ubayy ibn Kaʿb that al-Fatiha has no equal in the Torah, Gospel, Psalms, or Qur'an and is the seven oft-repeated verses.
rows.anchor: ما روى بأسانيد صحيحة عن أبي هريرة رضي الله تعالى عنه أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم خرج على أبي بن كعب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi calls al-Fatiha the Mother of the Book and a treasury of hidden knowledge and says some spiritual masters derive cosmic events and rulers' histories from it.
rows.anchor: فهي أم الكتاب والحاوية من دقائق الأسرار العجب العجاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Baqara is its common name, supported by a report from Ibn Masʿud; despite reports against naming suras this way, most permit it, perhaps because an early prohibition was later abrogated after Islam's strength grew.
rows.anchor: هذا هو الأسم المشهور وفي الصحيح عن إبن مسعود رضي الله تعالى عنه هذا مقام الذي أنزلت عليه سورة البقرة

rows.speaker: خالد بن معدان
rows.claim: Khalid ibn Maʿdan calls it the Qur'an's pavilion because of its greatness and its unique concentration of rulings; sayings ascribe to it a thousand commands, prohibitions, reports, and fifteen parables, and Ibn ʿUmar spent eight years learning it.
rows.anchor: وكان خالد بن معدان يسميها فسطاط القرآن

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: A report calls al-Baqara the best sura and Ayat al-Kursi its best verse; it is Medinan and has 286 verses according to the common count, with 287 also reported.
rows.anchor: وروى أن رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم قال : اي القرآن أفضل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The last revealed verse is “Be mindful of a day when you return to God,” revealed during the Farewell Pilgrimage on the Day of Sacrifice; that timing does not make it non-Medinan.
rows.anchor: وفيها آخر آية نزلت وهي قوله تعالى : ( وأتقوا يوما ترجعون فيه إلى الله )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Baqara follows al-Fatiha's sequence: knowledge of the Lord, worship, and requests for worldly and spiritual needs; al-Fatiha's request for guidance is echoed by “guidance for the God-conscious” at its opening.
rows.anchor: ووجه مناسبتها لسورة الفاتحة أن الفاتحة مشتملة على بيان الربوبية أولا والعبودية ثانيا وطلب الهداية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because al-Fatiha opened with the manifest, al-Baqara begins with hidden, mysterious letters whose secret is concealed except from whom God wills.
rows.anchor: ولما أفتتح سبحانه الفاتحة بالأمر الظاهر وكان وراء كل ظاهر باطن أفتتح هذه السورة بما بطن سره وخفى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi reads the command as revering God's names: do not force an interpretation without need, affirm an impossible literal meaning, apply a unique divine name to another, or use it in a way that equates God with others; avoid vulgar or irreverent settings and speech.
rows.anchor: سبح اسم ربك الأعلى أي نزه أسماءه عز وجل عما لا يليق

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik would tell a rejected petitioner simply that he had nothing to give, rather than invoking God, because he would not mention God's name to someone who disliked hearing it.
rows.anchor: وعن الإمام مالك رضي الله تعالى عنه أنه كان إذا لم يجد ما يعطي السائل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This first reading assumes “name” is not an inserted word; many instead treat it as an insertion that magnifies the divine referent, as in Labid's verse.
rows.anchor: وما ذكر من التفسير مبني على الظاهر من أن لفظ اسم غير مقحم وذهب كثير إلى أنه مقحم

rows.speaker: عقبة بن عامر الجهني
rows.claim: After the command to glorify God's great name was revealed, the Prophet told the Companions to use it in bowing; when the command to glorify the Most High came, he told them to use it in prostration.
rows.anchor: عن عقبة بن عامر الجهني قال لما نزلت فسبح باسم ربك العظيم قال لنا رسول الله

rows.speaker: إبن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas reports that when the Prophet recited this verse he said “Glory be to my Lord, the Most High.”
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس أن رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم كان إذا قرأ سبح اسم ربك الأعلى قال سبحان ربي الأعلى

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: When ʿAli said “Glory be to my Lord, the Most High” in prayer, he answered a question about adding to the Qur'an by explaining that he was merely carrying out the command.
rows.anchor: أن عليا كرم الله تعالى وجهه قرأ ذلك فقال سبحان ربي الأعلى وهو في الصلاة

rows.speaker: الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari explains the command as protecting God's names from heretical meanings such as determinism and anthropomorphism, as well as vulgarity and irreverent use.
rows.anchor: وفي الكشاف تسبيح اسمه تعالى تنزيهه عما لا يصح فيه من المعاني التي هي إلحاد في أسمائه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi says words used for divine names must be protected from obscenity and bad manners, and discusses criticism of Ibn al-Farid's poetic use of “Layla” and “Naʿm.”
rows.anchor: قال الإمام أنه كما يجب تنزيه ذاته تعالى وصفاته جلى وعلا عن النقائض يجب تنزيه الألفاظ الموضوعة لذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi discusses Ibn al-Farid poetry using Layla and Naʿm, criticized as irreverent, and a defense that treats the lines as allusive extended metaphor.
rows.anchor: ومن هذا يعلم ما في التعبير عنه تعالى شأنه بنحو ليلى ونعم كما يدعى ذلك في قول ابن الفارض قدس سره أبرق بدا من جانب الغور لامع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase may mean “naming of your Lord”: mention Him with reverence and treat His remembrance as honored.
rows.anchor: وقال الاسم بمعنى التسمية والمعنى نزه تسمية ربك بأن تذكره وأنت له سبحانه معظم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A defense of such poetry treats it as an extended metaphor with no word-by-word comparison; Alusi reports that critics reject this defense, while noting metaphorical allegory is used even for the basmala.
rows.anchor: والأظهر أن يقال إن الكلام المورد فيه ذلك من قبيل الأستعارة التمثيلية ولا نظر فيها إلى تشبيه المفردات بالمفردات

rows.speaker: إبن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas is reported to understand “glorify in the name of your Lord” as praying in His name, with the preposition omitted; Alusi doubts the report.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس أن المعنى صل باسم ربك الأعلى كما تقول ابدأ باسم الله تعالى

rows.speaker: عصام الدين
rows.claim: ʿIsam al-Din suggests that “name” means God's trace or effects, which point to Him as names do; Alusi finds this interpretation remote.
rows.anchor: وقال عصام الدين لا يبعد أن يراد الاسم الأثر أي أثر سبح آثار ربك الأعلى عن النقصان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If sabbiḥ means “sanctify,” either an inserted “name” or direct sanctification of names is possible; if it means “say subḥān,” “name” must be inserted, since no one says “glory to the name of my Lord.”
rows.anchor: وإذا كان معناه قل سبحان كما هو المعروف فيما بينهم فكونه مقحما متعين

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: A reading transmitted from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb says “Glory be to my Lord, the Most High,” supporting the interpretation of the command as uttering subḥān.
rows.anchor: ويؤيد هذا قراءة أبي بن كعب كما في خبر سعيد بن منصور وعبد بن حميد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi rejects the claim that the divine name and the named referent are identical, directing readers to his earlier discussion.
rows.anchor: وأما ما قيل من أن الاسم عين المسمى واستدل عليه بهذه الآية ونحوها فهو مما لا يعول عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Most High” describes God's power and dominion, not a location; alternatively, if it describes the name, that name is exalted above sharing its meaning with any other name.
rows.anchor: والأعلى صفة للرب وأريد بالعلو بالقهر والأقتدار لا بالمكان لاستحالته عليه سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relative clause “who created and proportioned” creates a syntactic problem if it modifies Lord, because another adjective intervenes, or if it modifies “name,” since names do not create; the preferred solution makes “Most High” an implied predicate or praise and leaves the object of “created” general.
rows.anchor: ( الذي خلق الخ إن كان صفة للرب كما هو الظاهر لزم الفصل بين الموصوف وصفته بصفة غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi takes “He created all things and proportioned them” broadly: God formed each creation as wisdom requires, with none perfected while another is not; specific readings are too restrictive.
rows.anchor: والمراد فجعل خلقه كما تقتضيه حكمته سبحانه في ذاته وصفاته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse's universal creation challenges Muʿtazilite claims that humans create their actions; al-Zamakhshari either avoids strict universality or says God enabled human action and bestowed their capacities.
rows.anchor: ورد بما دلت عليه الآية من العموم على المعتزلة في زعمهم أن العبد خالق لأفعاله

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi narrows creation and proportioning to every living creature, with its two hands, eyes, and legs made equal; Alusi says the textual ellipsis does not require such a restriction.
rows.anchor: وعن الكلبي خلق كل ذي روح فسوى بين يديه وعينيه ورجليه

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says God created the human and straightened its stature rather than making it inverted like cattle; Alusi likewise regards this as an unsupported narrowing.
rows.anchor: وعن الزجاج خلق الإنسان فعدل قامته ولم يجعله منكوسا كالبهائم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi's preferred reading is that God assigned exact measures to kinds, species, individuals, traits, acts, and lifespans, then guided each creature toward its natural or chosen outcome through inclinations, inspiration, signs, and revelation.
rows.anchor: جعل الأشياء على مقادير مخصوصة في أجناسها وأنواعها وأفرادها وصفاتها وأفعالها وآجالها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The varieties of guidance are extraordinary in plants and animals and still greater in humans, beyond the reach of description or compilation.
rows.anchor: وأما فنون هداياته سبحانه وتعالى للأنسان على الخصوص ففوق ذلك بمراحل

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other views say God shaped each creature, provided its livelihood, and guided it to religion and knowledge of divine unity; or assigned provisions and directed creatures to seek them.
rows.anchor: وقيل أي والذي قدر الخلق على ما خلقهم فيه من الصور والهيئات وأجرى لهم أسباب معاشهم

rows.speaker: مقاتل والكلبي
rows.claim: Muqatil and al-Kalbi say God determined creatures as male and female and guided the male in approaching the female.
rows.anchor: وعن مقاتل والكلبي قدرهم ذكرانا وإناثا وهدى الذكر كيف يأتي الأنثى

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says God measured humans and animals, guiding humans to good and evil and animals to grazing places.
rows.anchor: وعن مجاهد قدر الإنسان والبهائم وهدى الإنسان للخير والشر والبهائم للمراتع

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says God set the fetus's time in the womb at nine months, less, or more, and guided it to emerge fully formed.
rows.anchor: وعن السدي قدر الولد في البطن تسعة أشهر أو أقل أو أكثر وهداه للخروج منه للتمام

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation says God placed benefits in things and guided people to extract them; Alusi treats such specifications as examples of his broader reading, not limits on it.
rows.anchor: وقيل قدر المنافع في الأشياء وهدى الإنسان لاستخراجها والأولى ما ذكر أولا

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ claims the verse omits “and misled”; Alusi rejects this proposed ellipsis.
rows.anchor: وزعم الفراء في الآية اكتفاء والأصل فهدى وأضل وليس بشيء

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisaʾi reads qaddara with a light dāl, from ability or measuring.
rows.anchor: وقرأالكسائي قدر بالتخفيف من القدرة أو التقدير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God brought forth the grazing growth that animals eat, fresh, moist, and green; the surviving source text breaks off mid-word after describing its flourishing.
rows.anchor: أي أنبت ما ترعاه الدواب غضا رطبا يرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghuthāʾ is plant matter washed onto a valley's edge; the root can mean a mixture of diverse species, and the plural aghthāʾ is unusual.
rows.anchor: غثاء هو ما يقذف به السيل على جانب الوادي من الحشيش والنبات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here ghuthāʾ is dried vegetation; aḥwā means black or brown, though intense green is also explained as appearing black at first glance, supported by a line of Dhu al-Rumma.
rows.anchor: والمراد به هنا اليابس من النبات أي فجعله بعد ذلك يابسا أحوى من الحوة وهي كما قيل السواد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aḥwā may instead describe the fresh pasture as intensely green before it becomes debris; Alusi calls this reading less apparent.
rows.anchor: وجوز كونه حالا من المرعى أي أخرج المرعى حال كونه طريا غضا شديد الخضرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rapid sequence from freshness to dry debris emphasizes the abrupt change; the successive descriptions also express gradual growth and divine nurturing.
rows.anchor: وسر التقديم المبالغة في استعقاب حالة الجفاف حالة الرفيف والغضارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception is from all objects: the Prophet will remember what is recited to him except what God wills him to forget; Hasan, Qatada, and others say this refers to abrogation of both ruling and recitation.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن وقتادة وغيرهما وهذا مما قضى الله تعالى نسخه وأن يرتفع حكمه وتلاوته

rows.speaker: الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari treats forgetting as an allusion to God's lifting a verse's ruling and recitation, since what is withdrawn is left and eventually forgotten; Alusi sees no need for this figurative reading.
rows.anchor: وفي الكشاف أي إلا ما شاء الله فذهب به عن حفظك برفع حكمه وتلاوته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lifting a ruling or recitation can ordinarily cause people to stop reciting and remembering a verse, or can explain why God removes it from the Prophet's memory, so the causal language needs no strained interpretation.
rows.anchor: والمراد إما بيان السبب العادي البعيد للذهاب الله تعالى به عن الحفظ

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha reports that ten known sucklings were recited and then abrogated by five known sucklings; abrogation does not mean the Prophet forgot every such verse, since scholars retained some.
rows.anchor: أخرج الشيخان عن عائشة رضي الله تعالى عنها كان فيما أنزل عشر رضعات معلومات فنسخن بخمس معلومات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation says the Prophet hurried while Gabriel dictated and was told to wait for repeated recitation; Alusi says the obligation to remember after forgetting is not established by this verse.
rows.anchor: وقيل كان صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم يعجل بالقراءة إذا لقنه جبريل عليه السلام

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: A sound report says the Prophet omitted an āya while leading dawn prayer; Ubayy thought it had been abrogated, but the Prophet said he had forgotten it, and Alusi notes he would be reminded.
rows.anchor: وقد جاء في صحيح البخاري وغيره أنه صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم أسقط آية في قراءته في الصلاة

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ says God did not will that the Prophet forget anything, but the hypothetical exception shows divine power and teaches that his retention is God's favor; the possibility is known from elsewhere, including 20:114.
rows.anchor: فقال أنه تعالى ماشاء أن ينسى النبي صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم شيئا إلا أن المقصود من الإستثناء بيان أنه تعالى لو أراد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise negates lasting, uncorrected forgetting, not every lapse; the Prophet is not left forgetful of essential law, while correction can come through revelation or a listener's reminder.
rows.anchor: ثم أن المراد من نفي نسيان شيء من القرآن نفي النسيان التام المستمر مما لا يقر عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Invoking God's name emphasizes awe and signals that the divine will, bearing all attributes, governs the exception.
rows.anchor: والألتفات إلى الأسم الجليل على سائر الأوجه لتربية المهابة والإيذان بدوران المشيئة

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan links the promise to the Prophet's anxiety about forgetting while reciting to Gabriel; Alusi says a direct explanation or preparation for inspiration is more plausible.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حيان أنه سبحانه لما أمره صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم بالتسبيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clauses about divine knowledge can reinforce what precedes or what follows, or explain that God knows the Prophet's audible reading and fear and will preserve or let him forget what wisdom requires.
rows.anchor: إنه يعلم الجهر وما يخفى تعليل لما قبله والجهر هنا ما ظهر قولا أو فعلا أو غيرهما

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ reads the exception as a statement that God could make the Prophet forget if He wished, although He did not; it teaches that perfect retention is a divine gift, supported by 17:86 and 20:114.
rows.anchor: وبالجملة ففائدة هذا الإستثناء أن يعرفه الله تعالى قدرته حتى يعلم صلى الله عليه وسلم أن عدم النسيان من فضله

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan rejects readings that make the exception merely hypothetical or a negation, judging them unfitting for God's speech; Alusi calls that rejection extreme.
rows.anchor: وأباهما غاية الإباء لعدم الوقوف على حقيقتهما

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi says the Prophet is not allowed to remain forgetful of foundational law or duties, though he may be left to forget etiquette or sunnas.
rows.anchor: وقد ذكروا أنه عليه الصلاة والسلام لا يقر على النسيان فيما كان من أصول الشرائع والواجبات

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan connects the promise of recitation and protection from forgetting to the preceding command to glorify, because reciting the revealed Qur'an is necessary to glorification; Alusi finds the link weak.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حيان أنه سبحانه لما أمره صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم بالتسبيح وكان لا يتم إلا بقراءة ما أنزل عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi prefers treating “We shall make you recite” as an independent statement that explains why glorification is fitting or prepares the Prophet for divine inspiration, while signaling the blessing of glorification.
rows.anchor: ولو قيل أن سنقرئك استئناف واقع موقع التعليل للتسبيح أو للأمر به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “He knows what is open and hidden” explains God's management of recitation, preservation, and forgetting according to wisdom; other readings make it a general reinforcement or focus on the Prophet's audible recitation and anxiety.
rows.anchor: إنه يعلم الجهر وما يخفى تعليل لما قبله والجهر هنا ما ظهر قولا أو فعلا أو غيرهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi rejects attaching “He knows what is open and hidden” to the command to glorify as an explanation.
rows.anchor: وقيل إنه متعلق بقوله تعالى ( سبح اسم ربك الأعلى ) وهذا ليس بشيء كما ترى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise to ease the Prophet is coordinated with “We shall make you recite,” and the intervening verse is parenthetical; addressing the Prophet as the one eased suggests a firmly established capacity for it.
rows.anchor: ونيسرك لليسرى عطف على سنقرئك كما ينبيء عنه الألتفات إلى الحكاية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preferred broad sense is sustained divine enabling of the easiest way in every part of religion—knowledge, teaching, guidance, and being guided—including revelation, law, and perfecting the Prophet and others.
rows.anchor: أي نوفقك توفيقا مستمرا للطريقة اليسرى في كل باب من أبواب الدين علما وتعليقا واهتداء وهداية

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other views identify “the easiest way” as an easier way to retain revelation, the easy Hanif law, or good worldly and afterlife outcomes such as victory, status, and Paradise; adding religion broadens the last view.
rows.anchor: وقيل المراد باليسرى الطريقة التي هي أيسر وأسهل في حفظ الوحي وقيل هي الشريعة الحنيفية السهلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is to remind people through revelation and its legal teachings as God has enabled him; a second reading says to continue once revelation and his ease in religion are established, which Alusi accepts only if it means persistence.
rows.anchor: أي فذكر الناس حسبما يسرناك بما يوحى إليك واهدهم إلى ما في تضاعيفه من الأحكام الشرعية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The qualification “if the reminder benefits” means to focus on those from whom some benefit is hoped, because exhaustive reminders had only increased some people's disbelief and the Prophet's grief; he need not keep repeating to the hard-hearted after proof is conveyed.
rows.anchor: بأن يخص التذكير بمواد النفع في الجملة بأن يكون من يذكره كلا أو بعضا ممن يرجى منه التذكير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God informed the Prophet who was sealed in heart; after conveying the message and establishing proof, he need not repeatedly admonish those known to be impervious.
rows.anchor: فالشرط على هذا على حقيقته

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another reading treats the condition as rhetorical rather than literal: remind as commanded to earn reward even if the audience does not benefit, which also consoles the Prophet; Alusi prefers the literal condition.
rows.anchor: وقيل أنه ليس كذلك وإنما هو استبعاد النفع بالنسبة إلى هؤلاء المذكورين نعيا عليهم بالتصميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reminder will affect those disposed to fear God, or those who fear Him to some degree; the reminder deepens reflection until they recognize the truth and believe.
rows.anchor: سيذكر من يخشى أي سيذكر بتذكيرك من من شأنه أن يخشى الله تعالى حق خشيته

rows.speaker: الكوفيون
rows.claim: Some grammarians read in as “when,” citing Qur'anic and hadith usages; other grammarians deny that sense and answer their examples through alternative analysis.
rows.anchor: وقيل إن إن بمعنى إذ كما في قوله تعالى وأنتم العلون إن كنتم مؤمنين

rows.speaker: عصام الدين
rows.claim: ʿIsam al-Din says reminder should address what matters to each person: call unbelievers to faith before subsidiary duties, while reminding a sinful believer about prayer rather than faith.
rows.anchor: وقال عصام الدين المردا أن التذكير ينبغي أن يكون بما يكون مهما لمن له التذكير

rows.speaker: الفراء والنحاس والجرجاني والزهراوي
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ, al-Nahhas, al-Jurjani, and al-Zahrawi propose an ellipsis: remind whether or not the reminder benefits, as in a verse that mentions clothing protecting people from heat while omitting cold.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء والنحاس والجرجاني والزهراوي الكلام على الأكتفاء والأصل فذكر أن نفعت الذكر وإن لم تنفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional presents no difficulty for those who reject the converse implication of a condition.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الذين لا يقولون بمفهوم المخافة سواء كان مفهوم الشرط أو غيره لا يشكل عليهم أمر هذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who avoid the reminder avoid the admonition itself; al-ashqā is the unbeliever firmly denying resurrection or any premise that could produce fear of God.
rows.anchor: ويتجنبها أي ويتجنب الذكرى ويتحاماها الأشقى وهو الكافر المصر على إنكار المعاد

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view identifies the most wretched as the especially hostile unbeliever, such as al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and ʿUtba ibn Rabiʿa; a report says the verse was revealed about them.
rows.anchor: وقيل المراد الكافر المتوغل في عداوة الرسول صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم كالوليد بن المغيرة وعتبة بن ربيعة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other views take the term as all unbelievers, who are more wretched than sinners, or unbelievers of this community, whose believers are more blessed than earlier communities' believers; Alusi prefers the earlier interpretation.
rows.anchor: وقيل المراد به الكافر مطلقا فإنه أشقى من الفاسق وقيل المفضل عليه كفرة سائر الأمم

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ says “the greatest Fire” is the lowest layer of Hell; Alusi sees no difficulty in Hell having levels that differ in size and heat.
rows.anchor: أي الطبقة السفلى من أطباق النار كما قال الفراء ولا بعد في تفاضل نار الآخرة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan identifies the greatest Fire as the afterlife's Hellfire and the lesser fire as worldly fire; a marfuʿ report from Abu Hurayra says earthly fire is one seventieth of Hellfire, while an Ahmad version says one hundredth, perhaps using seventy as an expression of great number.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن الكبرى نار الآخرة والصغرى نار الدنيا ففي الصحيحين عن أبي هريرة مرفوعا ناركم هذه جزء منسبعين جزءا
